historical_timeline.summary: Baptized at Holy Trinity Church, Stratford-upon-Avon; the birth date is not recorded.
Twins Judith and Hamnet born; Hamnet dies at eleven.
Signs his revised will, three times.
Dies at Stratford; buried two days later. Cause unknown.
The vicar of Stratford records the story of a merry meeting and a fever.
Retrospective claims about pipe residues and about syphilis and mercury; both disputed.

claims.statement: William Shakespeare was born in Stratford-upon-Avon in April 1564; the exact date of his birth is not recorded, although it is most often celebrated on 23 April. His baptism is recorded in the parish register of Holy Trinity Church on Wednesday 26 April 1564 (Julian; 6 May 1564, Gregorian), in Latin, as 'Gulielmus filius Johannes Shakspere'. Baptisms typically took place within three days of birth.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The birth date is undocumented; 23 April is a tradition.

claims.statement: His father, John Shakespeare, was a glover who also traded in wool and lent money, served on the town council, and became high bailiff in 1568. Before William was born his parents had lost two infant daughters, Joan within the first few weeks of her life and Margaret a year after she was born; a younger sister, Anne, died at the age of eight.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Causes of these deaths are not recorded in the cited source.

claims.statement: At eighteen he married Anne Hathaway of Shottery; their daughter Susanna was born six months after the marriage, followed by the twins Judith and Hamnet in 1585. Hamnet died at the age of eleven.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The cause of Hamnet's death is not recorded in the cited source.

claims.statement: His wife and children remained in Stratford while he worked in London, and in 1597 he bought New Place, a large house in the centre of the town, which was his family home.

His will, made on 25 March 1616 (Julian; 4 April, Gregorian) and proved on 22 June 1616, opens with the words 'in perfect health and memory, God be praised', a typical phrase of the time. It is written on three sheets, each bearing his signature; these are three of the six surviving examples of his signature. Its first leaf has 'January' struck out and replaced with 'March', and scholars have suggested that it was drafted in January and revised on 25 March.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The formula does not establish his state of health.

claims.statement: The Folger Shakespeare Library describes the three signatures on the will as written in shaky strokes of the pen, suggestive of someone who had trouble holding a writing implement because of illness, and notes that if he was ill and signing from bed at an awkward angle the shakiness would not be remarkable; his other three signatures show similar slight variation. An archivist writing for The National Archives argued in 2016 that he was not seriously or chronically ill in January 1616 but probably fell seriously ill quite suddenly in late March and deteriorated over the next four weeks.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Interpretations of handwriting and of the will's revisions; no symptom is recorded, and other explanations (posture, age, the act of signing at the foot of a sheet) are offered by the same source.

claims.statement: He died at Stratford on 23 April 1616 (Julian; 3 May 1616, Gregorian), the date given on his monument in Holy Trinity Church, and his burial is recorded in the parish register on 25 April 1616 (Julian) as 'Will Shakspere gent.' The Shakespeare Birthplace Trust states that the cause of his death is not known.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Record the death as a fact; the cause is unknown.

claims.statement: John Ward, vicar of Stratford-upon-Avon and a physician, wrote in his notebook of 1662 to 1663 that 'Shakespeare, Drayton, and Ben Jonson had a merry meeting and it seems drank too hard for Shakespeare died of a fever there contracted'; the Folger Shakespeare Library calls it the only known account of his death.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Hearsay written down more than forty years after the death; often dismissed, though The National Archives' 2016 essay suggests it may deserve reconsideration. It is not evidence of his drinking habits.

claims.statement: A 2001 chemical study of 24 fragments of seventeenth-century clay pipes from Stratford-upon-Avon and its surroundings reported residues suggestive of cannabis in eight, four of them from the garden of his property, and of Peruvian cocaine in two, neither of which came from his property. The researchers stressed that the results do not show that he smoked any of these pipes.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The pipes cannot be linked to him or dated to his household; the cocaine-bearing pipes came from elsewhere.

claims.statement: A 2005 article in Clinical Infectious Diseases proposed, from his writings, the sonnets, and contemporary gossip, that he had syphilis and that a late-life decline in output, tremor, social withdrawal, and hair loss were due to mercury poisoning from its treatment.
claims.clinical_interpretation: A speculative hypothesis drawn from literary evidence; it was answered by letters in the same journal, and no documentary record of the disease, its treatment, or a tremor exists.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Evaluate a new tremor of the writing hand in a writer of 51: a history and examination that classify the tremor (rest, postural, kinetic; distribution; signs of parkinsonism, dystonia, or ataxia) against the MDS 2018 consensus; TSH, metabolic tests, and a medication, caffeine, and alcohol review with the AUDIT and a brief intervention for hazardous drinking; handwriting and Archimedes spiral samples and TETRAS ratings over time; propranolol, with primidone as the alternative, following the AAN 2011 guideline (reaffirmed 2025); occupational therapy for writing; a cold managed without decongestants on a beta-blocker; and prevention at 51, including vaccines, infection and fever precautions, and goals-of-care planning.

documentation.chief_complaint: Two-week review of tremor tests and alcohol; movement disorders neurology consultation today

hpi.narrative: Mr. Shakespeare returns two weeks after his first visit. He saw Dr. Osei-Carrow of movement disorders neurology this morning. Since the brief intervention he has had about 14 standard drinks a week, no more than four on any day, down from about 24; he notices that his hand is worst the morning after an evening of drinking and steadier for an hour after a glass of wine. He has had no sweats, anxiety, or craving on the lighter weeks. He has cut coffee to three cups a day. He brought a page of his handwriting from ten years ago and one written this morning: the recent script is larger, jagged, and drifts upward at the line ends. He has no slowness, stiffness, shuffling, change in his voice or face, loss of smell, constipation, or acting out of dreams. He takes no medicines.

assessment_plan.assessment: An isolated, bilateral action tremor of the upper limbs, present for at least three years by history and worse over six months, without head, voice, or leg tremor or any other neurological sign: essential tremor by the MDS 2018 criteria. TSH 1.6 mIU/L, glucose 92 mg/dL, calcium 9.4 mg/dL, sodium 139 mmol/L, and creatinine 0.96 mg/dL exclude thyroid and metabolic causes, and he takes no tremor-inducing medicine. Alcohol rebound and caffeine add an enhanced physiological component, and the brief improvement after a drink is typical of essential tremor. There are no signs of Parkinson disease. Dr. Osei-Carrow agrees. TETRAS performance 22 and activities of daily living 18; writing item 3

hpi.narrative: Mr. Shakespeare returns four weeks after starting propranolol extended-release 60 mg each morning. His hand is steadier: he can write a page before the script tires, though long drafts still ache and the signature at the foot of a page is the hardest part. He has had no dizziness, wheeze, cold hands, nightmares, low mood, or tiredness beyond the cold three weeks ago, which cleared without antibiotics or decongestants. He drinks about 10 standard drinks a week, no more than three on any day, and two cups of coffee. The occupational therapist's first appointment has not yet happened. He uses a heavier pen he bought himself.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Shakespeare is a 51-year-old man with essential tremor who started propranolol extended-release 60 mg one week ago and came in the same day with a cold. Two days ago he developed a sore throat and a blocked, running nose, then a dry cough; last night his temperature was 37.9 C. Several people at a reading he attended last week have had colds. He is eating and drinking normally. He has no shortness of breath, wheeze, chest pain, ear or facial pain, or rash. He bought a day-and-night cold remedy containing a decongestant and a night-time syrup with an antihistamine and alcohol, and asked whether he could take them with propranolol; he has not started them. On propranolol his hand is a little steadier, and he has had no dizziness, wheeze, or unusual tiredness. He has kept to about two drinks on most evenings and had none since the cold began.

In clinical terms: he named a close friend from the town as his health care agent and will complete the state directive form, which the clinic will scan into his chart; a copy can sit with his other papers. referral.question: A 51-year-old right-handed writer with six months of worsening tremor of the writing hand on a background of milder shaking for several years. Please classify the tremor, exclude early Parkinson disease and other causes, and advise on treatment
referral.urgency: Routine, within two to four weeks
referral.pertinent_history: Mr. Shakespeare is a 51-year-old playwright and poet who writes by hand first. For about three or four years he has noticed a slight shake when holding a full cup; over the past six months his handwriting has become larger, jagged, and tiring, and his signature is shaky. The tremor is worse when he is tired, after coffee, and the morning after an evening of drinking, and it eases for about an hour after a glass of wine. He has no rest tremor, slowness, stiffness, change in gait, voice, or smell, constipation, or dream enactment. He takes no medicines and has no asthma, heart block, or diabetes. He drinks about 24 standard drinks a week (AUDIT 12) without morning drinking or withdrawal; a brief intervention was given today with a goal of no more than 14 drinks a week and four on any day. He drinks four to five cups of coffee a day. He does not know of tremor in his family. On examination today: bilateral postural and kinetic hand tremor, right more than left, without rest tremor, bradykinesia, rigidity, or ataxia; pulse 80; blood pressure 134/84 mmHg. TSH, a metabolic panel, liver tests, and a blood count were drawn today
questions: What type of tremor is this, by the MDS consensus classification: essential tremor, an enhanced physiological tremor from alcohol or caffeine, or early Parkinson disease?
Is any imaging, such as brain MRI or dopamine transporter scanning, needed?
Do you advise propranolol, and at what dose and titration, or primidone instead?
What can he do to keep writing by hand, and is occupational therapy worthwhile?
How should his drinking, which briefly steadies the tremor, be addressed in the treatment plan?

consultant_note.history: Mr. Shakespeare is seen at the request of Dr. Achterberg-Sule, two weeks after his first visit. He describes a slight shake when holding a full cup for three or four years, and over six months a handwriting tremor that makes long drafts tiring and his signature unsteady; he brought a page from ten years ago and one written this morning, which show a clear change. The tremor appears with posture and action, not at rest, in both hands, worse on the right. It is worse with fatigue, coffee, and the morning after drinking, and eases for an hour after a glass of wine. He has no slowness, stiffness, falls, change in voice or facial expression, loss of smell, constipation, or dream enactment, and no head or leg tremor. He takes no medicines or supplements. Since his first visit he has cut his drinking to about 14 drinks a week and his coffee to three cups

assessment.assessment: An isolated tremor syndrome of bilateral upper-limb action tremor present for at least three years, without tremor elsewhere or other neurological signs: essential tremor by the MDS 2018 criteria. Thyroid and metabolic causes are excluded, and he takes no tremor-inducing drug. Alcohol rebound and caffeine add an enhanced physiological component, and the brief response to alcohol is typical of essential tremor. There are no features of Parkinson disease (no rest or re-emergent tremor, bradykinesia, or rigidity) or of dystonic tremor, so no imaging is needed
Alcohol steadies essential tremor for an hour or so and worsens it the next morning; using it as treatment risks escalating use, so it should be discussed openly as part of the tremor plan

recommendations: Propranolol extended-release 60 mg each morning, increasing after four weeks to 80 mg if the response is partial and the pulse allows, and up to 160 mg a day if needed; check pulse and blood pressure at each visit; do not stop it suddenly
If propranolol is not tolerated or does not help, primidone starting at 25 mg at night and increased slowly; not both at once for now
No brain MRI or dopamine transporter scan: the diagnosis is clinical and there are no atypical features
Occupational therapy for writing: weighted and wide-grip pens, forearm support, slower and larger script, and dictation for long drafts
Keep drinking within the agreed limits and do not use alcohol to settle the tremor; keep coffee to two cups a day, and avoid decongestants and other stimulants

TETRAS rating with a handwriting sample and spiral at each treatment review; ask me to see him again if a rest tremor, slowness, imbalance, or head or voice tremor appears, or if two first-line drugs fail, when surgical options would be discussed
